newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: HOWARD EXPECTS PROSSER TO "BEHAVE PROPERLY"
Prime Minister John Howard says he expects Small Business Minister Jeff Prosser to behave properly.
But Mr Howard is still backing his minister, saying he has every confidence in him.
Mr Howard says he doesn't believe Mr Prosser has breached any ministerial guidelines, and says the minister is devoting proper attention to his business.
But at a media conference in New York, the Prime Minister has refused to say if Mr Prosser is on his last chance.
Mr Howard said he will expect Mr Prosser to behave properly.
"I mean I choose to answer that question in that way because if I answer it in another way a certain erroneous assumption will be made about the basis of the response," Mr Howard said.
SYDNEY'S SECOND AIRPORT COULD BE AT GOULBURN
Hopes have been raised for Sydney's second international airport to be built at Goulburn, following a planned heritage listing at another proposed site for the facility.
The Australian Heritage Commission is expected to place the Holsworthy Army Base on an interim heritage listing, which could rule out plans for the aiport to be built at Holsworthy.
The move is being welcomed by a group planning to have the airport built at Goulburn.
Chairman of the Goulburn International Airport Committee, Peter Nightingale, says the Federal Government should acknowledge alternative proposed sites, other than Holsworthy and Badgery's Creek.
He says the heritage listing of Holsworthy will give Goulburn a better chance of being the chosen site.
SUGAR TARIFF ABOLISHED
The federal opposition says canegrowers can expect lower prices for their product when the sugar tariff is officially abolished tonight.
The Government has successfully defeated an Opposition motion to debate the scrapping of the tariff which was recommended in the sugar industry review.
Shadow Minister, Neil O'Keefe, says the removal of the $55 a tonne tariff will cost each Queensland canegrower thousands of dollars.
He says there will be a pay cut of around $20-million to growers in Queensland and $7-million to $8-million to growers in New South Wales, as of tomorrow morning.
The Canefarmers Association says it remains unconvinced the removal of the tariff will benefit the industry.
General Manager, John Allison, says it's unlikely to benefit the consumer either, because any reduction in sugar prices is a long way off.
He says there has been a review of a very competitive, efficient Australian industry, and money has been taken away from the farmer with no demonstrable benefit to the consumer.
ALICE SPRINGS NATIVE TITLE CLAIM BEGINS
A hearing into a native title claim over parts of Alice Springs begins in the Federal Court in the Central Australian town tomorrow.
Claimants will try to show the court they've had a continuing relationship with the land, despite efforts to sever the link.
Claimants want native title rights mainly over crown land within the town boundaries, including the Todd River bed and at the Telegraph Station.
The Alice Springs Arrente native title claim, will be heard by Justice Olney.
There will be three weeks of evidence, from the older claimants, followed by a week of cross-examination by the Northern Territory Government.
Claimants will be able to give evidence in groups and on visits to sites around the town.
The month-long sitting is just the beginning of the hearing, which is expected to resume in February next year.
CLOTHING INDUSTRY SLAMS RECOMMENDED TARIFF CUTS
Textile, clothing and footwear manufacturers say proposed tariff cuts will devastate the industry and consign 100,000 jobs to the dustbin.
The Productivity Commission has released a draft report recommending tariffs in the industry fall to 5 per cent by 2008.
Tariffs in the textile, clothing and footwear industries are due to fall to between 5-and-25 per cent by 2000, but the Commission says parts of the industry have been stifled by protection.
Executive Director of the Council of Textiles and Fashion Industries, Peter Kreitals, says the cuts are too fast.
Mr Kreitals says TCF industries contribute more to Australia's economy than car manufacturers, and deserve the same treatment from the government.
"We're asking for a pause in tariffs until 2005 and then we're happy for a continuation of reductions to meet our APEC timetable," he said.
The Textile, Clothing and Footwear Union says if the Government adopted the recommendations, 96,000 jobs would be lost.
National Secretary, Tony Woolgar, says in particular regional Australia would be devastated.
"We shouldn't be treated any differently, I mean there're more jobs at risk in TCF than what there were in vehicles. And at the end of the day it's all about jobs," he said.
The Federal Government has refused to comment on the Productivity Commission's report.
A spokesperson for Industry Minister John Moore says the Government will bear in mind the industry's concerns and Australia's free trade commitments, when it responds to the report.
Trade Minister Tim Fischer says the Government is committed to helping the industry boost its exports and become more internationally competitive.
JOBS MAY BE FOUND FOR MANY BHP WORKERS
The Australian Workers Union says BHP believes it can find jobs for more than 2,000 of its Newcastle workers who will be made redundant when steelmaking ends in the city in 1999.
Union official Kevin Marr says BHP told the Union last week, it hopes to find jobs for all but 200 of the workers, through re-training, internal transfers and attracting businesses to Newcastle.
He says BHP has based its job creation estimates on a recent survey of people employed at the Steelworks.
Mr Marr says after the talks last Friday, the Union is reasonably pleased with BHP's position on job security.
QUEENSLAND GOVERNMENT MOVE ON MOBILE PHONE TOWERS
The Queensland Government will put an interim regulation in place to control mobile phone towers and overhead cabling until the Federal Government comes up with guidelines for dealing with them.
Changes to the Telecommunications Act which take effect tomorrow will give State and Territory Governments control over telecommunications facilities.
The Australian Democrats are concerned the lack of guidelines means the States and Territories will not be able to control phone towers and cabling.
A spokesman for Local Government Minister, Di McCauley, says Queensland will introduce a local law councils will be able to adopt if they want to exercise controls over towers and cables.
He says the matter will also be addressed in planning laws later this year.
40 DAY PILGRIMAGE TO URANIUM SITES AROUND AUSTRALIA
Anti-nuclear activists are organising a 40 day pilgrimage to uranium sites around Australia, starting from Perth on August the 6th; Hiroshima Day.
The pilgrimage is being organised by a Perth group, the GAIA Foundation, which organises enviromental projects.
Ms Vallentine says there is particular concern about the proposal for Western Australia's first uranium mine, the CRA Kintyre project, near the Ruddall River National Park, in the State's north.
Kintyre will be the first stop for the Pilgrimage, followed by Jabiluka, in the Northern Territory, and other mine sites around Australia.
Ms Vallentine says there will be a core group of about 10 pilgrims, including two from overseas.
She says two people from the Chernobyl-affected area of Russia will talk with traditional Aboriginal custodians of proposed uranium mine sites.
